questions.stem: A 46 year old violinist has 3 years of shaking of both hands when he holds his bow or signs his name. It is absent when his hands rest in his lap. His father had a similar shake. Tone, power and speed of finger tapping are normal. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A bilateral action tremor, absent at rest, with a family history and no bradykinesia or rigidity is essential tremor.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: both hands when he holds his bow
His father had a similar shake
steps.x: Bilateral, on action, family history, no parkinsonism.

elim: Would come with ataxia, past-pointing and nystagmus.
Occurs with abnormal posturing, such as torticollis or writer's cramp.
Usually from anxiety, caffeine, drugs or thyrotoxicosis; the long family history fits ET.
Causes a unilateral rest tremor with bradykinesia and rigidity.

steps.x: Bilateral postural/action tremor + family history + no parkinsonian signs = essential tremor.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has a 2 year history of tremor of both hands. Her GP is unsure whether this is essential tremor or Parkinson's disease. She has no other medical problems and takes no regular medicines. Her TFTs are normal.
questions.q: Which examination finding would most support essential tremor?
o: Tremor on holding a posture that settles at rest, with normal tone
questions.e: Essential tremor is a postural and action tremor in the absence of parkinsonian features such as bradykinesia and rigidity; Parkinson's gives a resting tremor.

steps.x: The question asks: Which examination finding would most support essential tremor?
Separate the action tremor of ET from the rest tremor and parkinsonism of PD.

elim: A parkinsonian sign.
Bradykinesia, a parkinsonian sign.
A parkinsonian sign.
The classic Parkinson's tremor.

steps.x: ET: postural/action tremor, normal tone and speed. PD: rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man has a bilateral hand tremor that makes it hard to drink from a cup. Examination shows a postural tremor with normal tone and reflexes. He takes no medicines and drinks little coffee. His TFTs are normal. Several features of his history are recorded.
questions.q: Which feature of his history most supports a diagnosis of essential tremor?
o: He had a head injury aged 10
His mother and brother have the same tremor
The tremor started suddenly last week
questions.e: Essential tremor typically runs in families with autosomal dominant inheritance, so a positive family history is common and supportive.

steps.x: The question asks: Which feature of his history most supports a diagnosis of essential tremor?
The examination fits ET; look for the history feature that is typical of it.

elim: Not a recognised cause of a bilateral action tremor decades later.
Would point to drug-induced tremor, not ET; and he takes no medicines.
Non-specific.
ET is gradual and long-standing.

steps.x: ET is often familial (autosomal dominant). Ask about family history.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has a slow 'yes-yes' nodding movement of her head that has developed over 5 years. Her voice sounds shaky and she has a mild tremor of both outstretched hands. Her neck is not twisted or painful. Tone and finger tapping are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Essential tremor can involve the head (titubation, 'yes-yes' or 'no-no') and the voice, alongside a postural hand tremor.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: Tone and finger tapping are normal
steps.x: Head titubation, voice tremor and postural hand tremor with no parkinsonism.

elim: Causes twisting or tilting of the neck, often painful.
Causes chorea and cognitive change, not titubation.
Causes fatigable weakness, not tremor.
Can cause jaw or chin tremor, but not head titubation with normal tone and speed.

steps.x: ET can affect hands, head (titubation) and voice.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has a bilateral tremor of his hands that is worst when he holds them out in front of him. His father had the same. Examination shows normal tone and no bradykinesia. His tremor is recorded with accelerometry in a movement disorders clinic.
questions.q: Which is the most likely tremor frequency?
questions.e: Essential tremor has a frequency of 4 to 12 Hz, most commonly 6 to 8 Hz, worse with the arms outstretched.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely tremor frequency?

clues: worst when he holds them out
steps.x: A familial postural tremor.

elim: Far too slow for any common tremor.
Too slow for essential tremor.
Too fast; this is in the range of orthostatic tremor.
Too fast for a pathological tremor.

steps.x: ET frequency: 4 to 12 Hz, typically 6 to 8 Hz.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has a 7 year history of bilateral hand tremor that makes writing and holding a cup difficult. Her tone and speed of movement are normal. Her GP asks about factors that change the tremor to help confirm the diagnosis.
questions.q: Which feature of the tremor would most support essential tremor?
o: It came on with weight loss and heat intolerance
It improves after a glass of wine
It improves when she reaches for an object
It is worse when she reaches for a target and she past-points
It started after she began salbutamol
questions.e: Essential tremor is relieved by alcohol and other depressants, which helps distinguish it clinically.

steps.x: The question asks: Which feature of the tremor would most support essential tremor?
Action tremor with no parkinsonism; look for the classic modifier.

elim: Suggests thyrotoxicosis.
Rest tremor that settles on movement is Parkinson's.
Intention tremor with past-pointing is cerebellar.
Suggests drug-induced tremor.

steps.x: ET: better with alcohol, worse with caffeine.

questions.stem: A 22 year old student with known essential tremor says his hand tremor has become much worse during his exams. He is drinking four energy drinks and six coffees a day to stay awake. He sleeps 7 hours a night. He takes no medicines. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and his TFTs are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the worsening tremor?
questions.e: Stimulants such as caffeine worsen essential tremor; his intake is very high.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of the worsening tremor?

clues: four energy drinks and six coffees a day
steps.x: A huge stimulant intake.

elim: Alcohol usually improves essential tremor.
His TFTs are normal.
He sleeps 7 hours a night.
Propranolol treats ET, and he takes no medicines.

steps.x: Caffeine and other stimulants make ET worse.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man has had essential tremor for 20 years. He now spills soup, cannot do up his shirt buttons and has stopped eating in restaurants because he is embarrassed. His tone, power and gait are normal and his memory is good.
questions.q: Which is the main complication of his condition?
questions.e: Essential tremor is benign; its main complication is functional impairment from the tremor itself.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the main complication of his condition?

clues: cannot do up his shirt buttons
steps.x: Daily tasks are affected but examination is otherwise normal.

elim: ET is not a cerebellar degenerative disease.
His memory is good and dementia is not a typical complication.
His gait is normal.
ET is a benign condition, not a precursor of Parkinson's.

steps.x: ET's main complication = functional impairment.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has a tremor of both hands for 4 years. On finger-nose testing there is a tremor throughout the movement but she hits the target accurately. There is no nystagmus, no dysdiadochokinesia and her gait is normal. Tone is normal. Her mother had a tremor.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A bilateral action tremor with accurate targeting and no cerebellar or parkinsonian signs, plus a family history, is essential tremor.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Action tremor without cerebellar signs.

elim: Would worsen near the target with past-pointing, nystagmus and dysdiadochokinesia.
She has no new medicines in the history.
Would give cerebellar or other focal neurological signs.
Causes a rest tremor with rigidity, not an action tremor with normal tone.

steps.x: ET: bilateral action tremor, no cerebellar or parkinsonian signs.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has a 3 year history of shaking of both hands when he eats with a spoon. His sister has the same problem. He takes no medicines and his TFTs are normal. He is examined in the neurology clinic.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Bilateral postural tremor with normal tone and speed of movement
Bradykinesia with decrement on finger tapping
questions.e: In essential tremor the examination shows a bilateral tremor, worse with action, with no rigidity or bradykinesia.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination?

clues: both hands when he eats with a spoon
His sister has the same problem
steps.x: Familial bilateral action tremor.

elim: A parkinsonian sign.
A parkinsonian sign.
Cerebellar signs.
Typical of Parkinson's disease.

steps.x: ET examination: bilateral action tremor, no rigidity, no bradykinesia.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman with a bilateral hand tremor is seen by her GP. Her mother had a similar tremor. Examination shows normal tone and normal speed of movement. The GP asks her which everyday activities make the tremor most obvious.
questions.q: Which activity is most likely to make her tremor worse?
o: Sitting with her hands resting in her lap
Walking with her arms by her sides
questions.e: Essential tremor is more noticeable during voluntary movement and sustained posture, for example pouring a drink.

steps.x: The question asks: Which activity is most likely to make her tremor worse?

clues: Her mother had a similar tremor
steps.x: A familial bilateral tremor.

elim: Tremors disappear in sleep.
A rest tremor of Parkinson's disease appears here; ET does not.
The resting arm tremor of Parkinson's disease often appears when walking.
Her hands are at rest.

steps.x: ET is worse with action, for example pouring a drink.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has a quavering, shaky voice that has developed over 4 years. She also has a mild tremor of both outstretched hands. Her speech is not slurred, swallowing is normal, her tongue looks normal and her voice does not fade with prolonged talking.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her voice change?
o: Essential tremor affecting the laryngeal muscles
questions.e: Essential tremor can involve the voice through the laryngeal muscles, typically with a postural hand tremor.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her voice change?

clues: does not fade with prolonged talking
steps.x: Voice tremor plus postural hand tremor.

elim: Would cause slurred speech, dysphagia and tongue fasciculations.
Speech fatigues with prolonged talking.
Causes quiet monotonous speech with bradykinesia, not a vocal tremor with normal speed.
Causes a hoarse, weak voice, not a tremulous one.

steps.x: ET can affect the voice (laryngeal muscles) and head.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a 5 year history of bilateral hand tremor on holding objects. His father had the same. He has no rigidity, no bradykinesia and no cerebellar signs. His TFTs are normal. He asks for a brain scan to confirm the diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Essential tremor is a clinical diagnosis; imaging does not confirm it.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?

clues: no rigidity, no bradykinesia and no cerebellar signs
steps.x: A typical case with no signs of another cause.

elim: Does not diagnose essential tremor.
Used when parkinsonism is uncertain; he has no parkinsonian signs.
Not useful for tremor diagnosis.
Normal in essential tremor and not needed for a typical case.

steps.x: ET is diagnosed clinically. No scan is needed for a typical case.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has a 3 month history of bilateral hand tremor on holding a cup. She has no family history of tremor. She feels on edge and has had looser stools. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm. There is no rigidity or bradykinesia.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: If the diagnosis of essential tremor is uncertain, exclude other causes such as thyroid disease; her tachycardia and loose stools suggest thyrotoxicosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
A short history, no family history and features of thyrotoxicosis make ET uncertain.

elim: There are no parkinsonian features.
No gene test is used to diagnose ET.
Not first-line for a bilateral postural tremor without focal signs.
Not used to assess tremor.

steps.x: Uncertain diagnosis: check TFTs to exclude thyroid disease.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has a 6 year history of tremor of both hands when writing. His mother had the same tremor. Examination shows a postural tremor with normal tone and no bradykinesia. Investigations are shown. He drinks two cups of tea a day and takes no medicines. His pulse rate is 72 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: With thyroid disease excluded and a typical history and examination, essential tremor is diagnosed clinically.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?

clues: His mother had the same tremor
steps.x: Typical ET and a normal thyroid screen.

elim: Not needed for a typical ET picture.
Only if parkinsonism is uncertain.
Not needed for a typical ET picture.
His TFTs are already normal and the picture is typical.

steps.x: Clinical diagnosis; investigations only to exclude other causes.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman describes shaking of both hands that is worse when holding a newspaper. Her father had a similar problem. Her hands look still when they rest on her knees. The doctor wants a bedside test to show the tremor during the examination.
questions.q: Which bedside manoeuvre is most likely to show her tremor?
o: Lying flat with her eyes closed
questions.e: Essential tremor is an involuntary oscillation that is exacerbated with the arms outstretched.

steps.x: The question asks: Which bedside manoeuvre is most likely to show her tremor?
A postural tremor that disappears at rest.

elim: Tests UMN pathways above the pons, not tremor.
Tremor settles at rest.
Tests proprioception, not tremor.
Sensory testing does not show tremor.

steps.x: Show ET by holding the arms outstretched, then do an action task.

questions.stem: A 44 year old teacher has essential tremor that makes writing on the board and marking difficult. She has no asthma, heart block or other medical problems. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. She would like treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: Propranolol is first-line for essential tremor when it is not contraindicated.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

clues: makes writing on the board and marking difficult
steps.x: Functionally limiting ET with no contraindication to a beta-blocker.

elim: For severe, refractory cases only.
Treats Parkinson's disease, not ET.
The alternative when propranolol is contraindicated, as in asthma.
A second-line option.

steps.x: ET first-line = propranolol; primidone if asthma.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man with essential tremor started propranolol 2 weeks ago. He has developed wheeze and night-time cough, and spirometry now shows reversible airflow obstruction consistent with asthma. His tremor had improved. His oxygen saturation is 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Add a salbutamol inhaler and continue propranolol
questions.e: Propranolol is contraindicated in asthma, so primidone is used as the alternative.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
New asthma while taking a non-selective beta-blocker.

elim: Propranolol is contraindicated in asthma.
Only for severe refractory tremor.
Would worsen bronchospasm.
Still a beta-blocker; the alternative for ET in asthma is primidone.

steps.x: Asthma: no propranolol. Use primidone.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman has essential tremor that stops her drinking from a cup. Propranolol did not help at full dose, and primidone made her too drowsy to continue. She has no asthma or other medical problems. Her tremor is moderate and she does not want surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
questions.e: When propranolol and primidone fail, other options include topiramate, gabapentin and clonazepam.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
Both first-line drugs have failed; surgery declined.

elim: Used in Parkinson's disease, not ET.
For severe refractory tremor; she does not want surgery.
Can cause drug-induced parkinsonism; not used for ET.
Treats Parkinson's disease.

steps.x: ET second-line: topiramate, gabapentin or clonazepam.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with essential tremor has had to stop propranolol because of fatigue and primidone because of unsteadiness. He has kidney stones, so topiramate is avoided. He still struggles to shave and eat. His pulse rate is 70 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
questions.e: Second-line options for essential tremor include topiramate, gabapentin and clonazepam; with topiramate avoided, gabapentin is appropriate.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
First-line drugs failed and topiramate is unsuitable.

elim: A dopamine agonist, not used for ET.
Treats Parkinson's disease.
Not used for ET and may cause parkinsonism.
Can cause tremor rather than treat it.

steps.x: Other ET options: topiramate, gabapentin, clonazepam.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has severe essential tremor. She cannot feed herself or write. She has had adequate trials of propranolol, primidone, topiramate and gabapentin without benefit. She has no cognitive impairment and is otherwise fit. Her BP is 130/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Restart propranolol at a lower dose
questions.e: Severe essential tremor refractory to medication is treated with deep brain stimulation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?
Severe disabling tremor despite several drugs.

elim: Sedation is not an acceptable treatment endpoint.
Does not treat ET.
Alcohol's effect is short-lived and it is not a treatment strategy.
Already failed at an adequate dose.

steps.x: Refractory severe ET = deep brain stimulation.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man with essential tremor says his tremor settles for about an hour after two pints of beer, so he now drinks before meetings and meals. He drinks 30 units a week. He has no asthma. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Advise reducing alcohol and start propranolol
Continue alcohol as it treats the tremor
questions.e: Alcohol relieves essential tremor only briefly and is not a treatment; propranolol is first-line.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?

clues: settles for about an hour after two pints of beer
steps.x: He is using alcohol to self-treat and drinks above safe limits.

elim: Alcohol's effect is short-lived and it is not a treatment strategy.
Reserved for severe refractory tremor.
Primidone is the alternative in asthma; he has no contraindication to propranolol.
Treats Parkinson's disease, not ET.

steps.x: Alcohol improves ET briefly but is not a treatment. First-line drug: propranolol.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has a long-standing bilateral postural tremor of her hands and a 'no-no' head tremor. Her father and grandmother had the same. Her MRI brain is normal. She asks which part of the brain causes her tremor.
questions.q: Which is the most likely origin of her tremor?
o: Abnormal oscillation in the cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit
Dopaminergic loss in the substantia nigra
questions.e: Essential tremor is thought to arise from abnormal oscillatory activity in the cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit; the exact mechanism is incompletely understood and it is usually autosomal dominant.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely origin of her tremor?

clues: Her father and grandmother had the same
steps.x: Familial postural tremor with normal imaging.

elim: Causes LMN weakness and fasciculations, as in MND.
Causes sensory ataxia, not tremor.
The cause of the rest tremor of Parkinson's disease.
Causes hemiballismus.

steps.x: ET: cerebello-thalamo-cortical oscillation.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has essential tremor. His friend has Parkinson's disease, and he notices his friend's hand shakes when resting on the arm of a chair, whereas his own hand only shakes when he lifts a cup. He asks why their tremors differ.
questions.q: Which best explains why his tremor occurs on action rather than at rest?
o: Dysfunction is in circuits maintaining posture and voluntary movement
He has basal ganglia dopaminergic degeneration
His tremor is caused by anxiety
questions.e: Parkinson's produces a resting tremor from basal ganglia dopaminergic pathology, whereas ET reflects dysfunction in circuits that maintain limb posture and voluntary movement.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains why his tremor occurs on action rather than at rest?

clues: shakes when resting on the arm of a chair
only shakes when he lifts a cup
steps.x: Rest tremor (friend) versus action tremor (him).

elim: This causes the resting tremor of Parkinson's disease.
Neuropathy does not explain an action tremor of this type.
Tone is normal in ET.
ET is a neurological circuit disorder.

steps.x: PD = basal ganglia, rest tremor. ET = posture/movement circuits, action tremor.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman with essential tremor notices that her tremor almost disappears for an hour after a glass of wine at dinner, then returns. She asks why alcohol has this effect and whether she should use it regularly.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the improvement with alcohol?
o: Increased dopamine release in the striatum
Suppression of abnormal cerebellar and olivary oscillation
questions.e: Alcohol is thought to suppress abnormal cerebellar and olivary oscillatory activity; the effect is short-lived and it is not a treatment strategy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of the improvement with alcohol?
Brief improvement with alcohol.

elim: This is how propranolol is thought to help.
Not the mechanism; ET is not dopaminergic.
Does not explain tremor suppression.
She is awake and the effect is specific to the tremor.

steps.x: Alcohol damps cerebellar/olivary oscillation briefly. It is not a treatment.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with essential tremor starts the first-line drug for his condition. His tremor improves over 2 weeks. His resting pulse falls from 80 to 64 bpm. He asks which receptors the tablet acts on. He has no asthma. His BP is 128/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which receptors does this drug act on to reduce his tremor?
questions.e: Propranolol blocks beta-adrenergic receptors, reducing peripheral beta-adrenergic enhancement of tremor; this overlaps with the amplification seen in ET.

steps.x: The question asks: Which receptors does this drug act on to reduce his tremor?
The first-line drug is propranolol, and the falling pulse confirms beta-blockade.

elim: Targeted by antipsychotics, and D2 agonists treat Parkinson's.
Benzodiazepines such as clonazepam act here.
Anticholinergics act here; not first-line for ET.
Not the mechanism of first-line ET treatment.

steps.x: Propranolol blocks beta-adrenergic enhancement of tremor.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has essential tremor. His father and paternal grandfather also have it. His wife is pregnant with their first child and has no tremor or family history of tremor. They ask about the risk to the baby.
questions.q: Which is the chance that their child inherits the condition?
questions.e: Essential tremor is typically autosomal dominant, so each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting it.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the chance that their child inherits the condition?
Vertical transmission through males, so autosomal dominant.

elim: ET is usually inherited, so the risk is not zero.
Only one parent carries the gene.
This is the risk when both parents are carriers of an autosomal recessive condition.
That would suggest X-linked inheritance; ET is autosomal dominant.

steps.x: ET is autosomal dominant: 50% risk to each child.

questions.stem: A 42 year old accountant has a mild bilateral postural hand tremor that he notices only when tired. His father had the same. It does not affect his writing, typing, eating or work, and he is not embarrassed by it. He has no other medical problems. His TFTs are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Explanation and reassurance without drug treatment
questions.e: Essential tremor is benign and treatment is aimed at functional impairment; a mild tremor that does not limit function needs explanation only, with propranolol if it starts to interfere.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?

clues: does not affect his writing, typing, eating or work
steps.x: Mild tremor with no functional impact.

elim: Reserved for severe, refractory tremor.
Treats Parkinson's disease, not ET.
Drug treatment is not needed while the tremor causes no functional impairment.
A second-line drug; not needed for mild tremor.

steps.x: Treat ET when it impairs function; first-line is then propranolol.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has 8 months of tremor of his left hand. His family say he has slowed down and his writing has become smaller. He has no family history of tremor. Examination shows increased tone in the left arm. His TFTs are normal. Essential tremor is considered.
questions.q: Which finding makes the diagnosis of essential tremor least likely?
o: Increased tone with slowing of movement
questions.e: Essential tremor is defined by the absence of parkinsonian features; rigidity, slowness and micrographia point to Parkinson's disease, making the diagnosis uncertain.

steps.x: The question asks: Which finding makes the diagnosis of essential tremor least likely?

clues: increased tone in the left arm
steps.x: Bradykinesia, micrographia and rigidity are parkinsonian features.

elim: This supports, rather than excludes, essential tremor.
ET can start at any age, including later life.
This is typical of ET.
This is typical of ET.

steps.x: ET requires no rigidity or bradykinesia. If they are present, think again.
